questions.explanation: False Statements Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks Explanation: This is false because the Banker's algorithm is used for Deadlock Avoidance , not prevention. Prevention involves negating one of the four necessary conditions (like Hold and Wait), while Avoidance dynamically checks for a safe sequence. An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource Explanation: This is false. In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG), an Assignment Edge goes from Resource $\rightarrow$ Process , showing the resource is held. An edge from Process $\rightarrow$ Resource is a Request Edge . True Statements Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed Explanation: True. Forcing a process to request all resources at once (or only when it has none) breaks the "Hold and Wait" condition, effectively preventing deadlocks. questions.explanation: The Deadlock-Free Formula The standard formula for a system with $n$ processes and a single resource type where each process P has a maximum requirement m is: Step-by-Step Calculation Identify the variables: * Number of processes (n) = 5. Maximum requirement for each process (m) = 2. Calculate the "Worst-Case" allocation: A deadlock occurs if every process holds one less than its maximum requirement and no resources are left. Each process holds (2 - 1) = 1 instance. Total instances held by all 5 processes in this state = 5 *1 = 5. Find the minimum k: To break the deadlock, you need at least one more resource so that one process can finish. k = 5 + 1 = 6. questions.questionText: Three processes $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ are given. Two binary semaphores are initialized as $(A=2)$ and $(B=0)$. A shared variable $(x)$ is initialized as $(x=0)$. Each process executes the following code: wait(A); printf("*"); x = x + 1; if (x == 2) { printf("$"); signal(B); } wait(B); signal(A); printf("#"); signal(B); Which of the following outputs is possible? $***\$\#\#\#$ $**\$*\#\#\#$ $**\$\#*\#\#$ $**\$\#\#*\#$
questions.questionHtml:
Three processes $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ are given. Two binary semaphores are initialized as $(A=2)$ and $(B=0)$. A shared variable $(x)$ is initialized as $(x=0)$.

Each process executes the following code:

wait(A);
printf("*");
x = x + 1;
if (x == 2) { 
    printf("$"); 
    signal(B);
}
wait(B);
signal(A);
printf("#");
signal(B);

Which of the following outputs is possible?

  1. $***\$\#\#\#$
     
  2. $**\$*\#\#\#$
     
  3. $**\$\#*\#\#$
     
  4. $**\$\#\#*\#$
questions.explanation: Given Processes: P1, P2, P3 Semaphores: A = 2 (counting semaphore) B = 0 Shared variable x = 0 Each process executes: wait(A); printf("*"); x = x + 1; if (x == 2) { printf("$"); signal(B); } wait(B); signal(A); printf("#"); signal(B); Important Observations A = 2 → Only two processes can enter initially . → The third process waits . Each process prints: one "*" one "#" So total output must contain: 3 stars (*) 3 hashes (#) "$" prints only once because it prints when x == 2 . B = 0 initially → All processes block at wait(B) until the process where x = 2 executes signal(B) . Step-by-Step Execution (Typical Case) Step 1 Two processes enter (say P1 and P2 ). P1: wait(A) → print * P2: wait(A) → print * Output: ** Step 2 Update x P1 → x = 1 P2 → x = 2 When x = 2 printf("$") signal(B) Output: **$ Step 3 Now B = 1 , so one process continues past wait(B) . Example order: P2 continues signal(A) print # signal(B) Output **$# Step 4 Second process passes wait(B) P1 continues signal(A) print # sig

questions.questionHtml:
A computer system supports a logical address space of $2^{32}$ bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of $4096$ bytes. A logical address is divided into a $b$-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of $b$ is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Logical Address Space $= 2^{32}$ Bytes Page Size $= 4096$ Bytes $= 2^{12}$ Bytes Page Table Entry Size $($at inner page table$)$ $= 8$ Bytes $= 2^{3}$ Bytes It is given that there is two-level hierarchical paging, with $b-$bit index to the outer page table. Now, as given all pages in the system have the same size. So, $1$ Page Table should fit in $1$ Page. Therefore, Page Table Size $=$ Page Size. Page Table Size $= 2^{12}$ Bytes Page Table Size $=$ No. of Entries $\times$ Page Table Entry Size So,  No. of Entries $\times$ Page Table Entry Size $= 2^{12}$ Bytes No. of Entries at inner level$= \frac{2^{12}}{2^{3}} = 2^{9} $ As, no. of entries are $2^{9}$ at inner level, $9$ bits would be required for index at that level. So, $x=9$ $b+x+12 = 32$ $b=32-12-9$ $b=11$ Answer : Value of $\mathbf{b}$ is $\mathbf{11}$    benzene06 answered Feb 28, 2025 • edited Feb 28, 2025 by benzene06 benzene06 comment Share Follow See all 15 Comments 15 15 Comments reply Show 12 pre

questions.questionText: A computer has two processors, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. Four processes $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ with CPU bursts of $20,16,25$, and $10$ milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows: $M_{1}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{1}>P_{3}>P_{2}>P_{4}$, i.e., $P_{1}$ and $P_{4}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively. $M_{2}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{2}>P_{3}>P_{4}>P_{1}$, i.e., $P_{2}$ and $P_{1}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively. A process $P_{i}$ is scheduled to a processor $M_{k}$, if the processor is free and no other process $P_{j}$ is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds? $9.00$ $8.75$ $6.50$ $7.50$
questions.questionHtml:
A computer has two processors, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. Four processes $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ with CPU bursts of $20,16,25$, and $10$ milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

  • $M_{1}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{1}>P_{3}>P_{2}>P_{4}$, i.e., $P_{1}$ and $P_{4}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
  • $M_{2}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{2}>P_{3}>P_{4}>P_{1}$, i.e., $P_{2}$ and $P_{1}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process $P_{i}$ is scheduled to a processor $M_{k}$, if the processor is free and no other process $P_{j}$ is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?

  1. $9.00$
  2. $8.75$
  3. $6.50$
  4. $7.50$
questions.explanation: Processes and Burst Times: P₁ → 20 ms P₂ → 16 ms P₃ → 25 ms P₄ → 10 ms All arrive at time 0 . Time 0: Both processors free M₁ will prefer P₁ (highest priority) M₂ will prefer P₂ (highest priority)  Assign: M₁ → P₁ (20 ms) M₂ → P₂ (16 ms) Time 16: M₂ becomes free Only P₃ and P₄ remain. So, the amount of data that can be stored in a data block will be 65536-4=65532 Bytes . We are asked to store 1MB (2^20 B) file on the disk, which can be stored in ceil (2^20/65532)= 17 blocks . Here, block no. 1 to 16 would be completely occupied with 65532 bytes file data , and the 17th block occupied with remaining 64 bytes of file data, leaving a space of 65532-64=65468 Bytes that would be wasted due to internal fragmentation. Hence, the amount of space that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is 65468 Bytes. questions.explanation: A: True If a process itself makes a block() call, then it will be blocked until the I/O operation completes. B: True If a page is not in the physical memory, then the OS invokes the Page Fault Handler , and the process remains blocked until the page is read (i.e., the disk I/O is complete). questions.explanation: As far as I remember the question the answer should be the process moving from waiting to running state. We were asked to pick the false one out. Another options were : Option 1: Ready to running Option 2: Running to ready (This is when preemptive OS is used.) Option 3: Waiting to running and one more option (I am unable to recall) Only waiting to running is not possible. According to you, process can't go to I/O first as the request for I/O can only be made once the process request for the I/O after being getting in the running queue. Without being in the running queue OS can never decide what I/O device a particular process need. So I think the correct statement should be if a process perform I/O time then it needs to switch from running to waiting and then from waiting to ready and then ready to running.

Which one or more of the following need to be saved on a context switch from one thread $\text{(T1)}$ of a process to another thread $\text{(T2)}$ of the same process?

  1. Page table base register
  2. Stack pointer
  3. Program counter
  4. General purpose registers

options.text: Stack pointer

options.label: C
options.text: Program counter

options.label: D
options.text: General purpose registers

questions.explanation: Answer: B, C, D Page table base register : This register holds the base address of the page table for the currently executing thread. Since all the threads of a process share the same page table , this register needs needs not be saved . Stack pointer: This register points to the top of the stack for the currently executing thread. Since each thread has its own stack , the stack pointer needs to be saved and restored on a context switch to ensure that the new thread uses the correct stack. Program counter: This register contains the address of the next instruction to be executed by the currently executing thread. To resume execution of the new thread, the saved program counter needs to be loaded into the program counter register. General purpose registers : These registers are used to store temporary data and intermediate results during the execution of a thread. Since the state of these registers can be different for each thread, they need to be saved and restored on a context switch

questions.explanation: Ans: Option C According to Galvin, “The TLB is associative, high-speed memory. Each entry in the TLB consists of two parts: a key (or tag) and a value. When the associative memory is presented with an item, the item is compared with all keys simultaneously. If the item is found, the corresponding value field is returned.” Hence option A is TRUE.    The TLB contains only a few of the page-table entries. If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit it means the the page number is found, so its frame number is immediately available and is used to access memory.
